analyst_note: Manual source-code verification pass. All critical findings reviewed against actual file content ±10 lines.

findings.rationale: Three unguarded std::system() calls at lines 663, 672, 685 interpolate iface.c_str() into a shell command string via snprintf. If interface_name originates from external input (config file, API), arbitrary shell commands can execute. The NOLINT suppressor acknowledges but does not fix the risk. No sanitization or allowlist check present.
Second unguarded std::system() call in applyTrafficShaping(). Same root cause as line 663 — iface flows directly into shell cmd without allowlist validation.

Third std::system() call. Rate value also interpolated. Both the interface name and rate_kbps require sanitization. Fix: replace with execv()-family call with explicit argv[] array, or use netlink(7) sockets directly.

findings.pattern: defaultHealthCheck stub opens no real TCP connection; comment says 'in a real implementation this would open a TCP connection'
findings.rationale: defaultHealthCheck() is the fallback used when no health_check_fn_ is registered. It always returns true without testing the backend. In production this means dead backends pass health checks. Comment at line 426-429 explicitly admits the function is not implemented. All db_connection_leak scanner hits (lines 288-290) originate from this stub: because connections are never tested or tracked, any future implementation that does open connections will need RAII guards.

~MemoryMappedPayload() at line 393 is correctly marked noexcept-compatible (no throw statements). The constructor throws (lines 296-349) but not the destructor. The scanner flagged line 220 which is inside writeTo(), not a destructor. RAII move semantics are correctly implemented. Downgrade: no actual exception-throwing destructor exists — the gap is a constructor that must be called inside try-catch at call sites.

findings.pattern: Sequential lock on connections_mutex_ then rate_limit_mutex_ in accept path
findings.rationale: checkConnectionLimit() acquires connections_mutex_ (line 701); immediately after, checkRateLimit() acquires rate_limit_mutex_ (line 710). In the accept handler these are called sequentially. A second code path (registerConnection line 751 + updateStats line 830) acquires connections_mutex_ then stats_mutex_. If any thread holds stats_mutex_ and tries to acquire connections_mutex_ a cycle is possible. Fix: establish and enforce canonical lock ordering (connections < rate_limit < stats).

findings.pattern: Nested connections_mutex_ acquisition after outer connections_mutex_ scope in same accept loop
findings.rationale: registerConnection() (line 751) and active_sessions_.try_emplace (line 855) each acquire connections_mutex_ as separate, non-nested scopes within the same accept handler — they are safe individually but the ordering relative to stats_mutex_ (lines 830, 845) creates an ABBA opportunity with concurrent stat-reading threads.

SocketTimeoutManager manages socket handles and timers but no destructor definition was found in the cpp (header-only inline dtor candidate). If the class holds OS socket_t resources, relying on implicit destructor risks leaking handles on abnormal shutdown. Needs explicit destructor with handle cleanup.

The scanner flagged lines 175 and 194 as missing_dtor, but these are actually brace-closing lines for an #ifdef __linux__ setsockopt block. The actual destructor at line 63 is correctly marked noexcept and calls stop(). The no_timeout on the SO_SNDTIMEO path applies only to Linux and the 5s value is hardcoded — configurable timeout would be preferable but not critical.

Line 194 is the closing brace of a Linux-only setsockopt block, not a destructor. Scanner misidentified the brace structure. The real concern is the hardcoded 5s SO_SNDTIMEO; downgraded to HIGH for the hardcoded constant, not a missing destructor.

Accept loop (line 208) does use a 30-second deadline via steady_clock comparison at line 243. The timeout IS implemented. However it uses a polling sleep_for(poll_interval) rather than an async timer, creating up to poll_interval latency per iteration. Downgrade: timeout exists but mechanism is suboptimal.

Line 202 uses a ternary to select between two std::chrono::milliseconds values, not a smart pointer at all — however the header for SocketTimeoutManager stores raw socket_t handles alongside std::shared_ptr members. The scanner likely fired on the .get() call pattern for a shared_ptr wrapping a raw handle. Real risk: if the shared_ptr's custom deleter is missing or incorrect, the OS socket leaks.

R12 bounds checks have been added at lines 108-113: offset > concat.size() and samples[i].size() > (concat.size()-offset) both guard the memcpy at line 115. The scanner fired on the memcpy line but the preceding guard makes it safe. Downgrade to MEDIUM: verify that concat.size() is validated against total expected size before the loop.

R13 bounds checks wrap all four memcpy calls (lines 250, 257, 264, 271). Each offset + sizeof check guards before copy. Line 251 is actually a return false after a bounds check, not the memcpy. Scanner fired on adjacent line. Downgrade to MEDIUM: SQE_SIZE is a compile-time constant; static_assert would be stronger than runtime checks.

braces_imbalance_at_line_1.root_cause: Scanner's file-level brace heuristic fires on #ifdef/#endif preprocessor blocks that have balanced braces per-platform but appear imbalanced to a naive counter that does not model conditional compilation. All 5 files verified balanced by stripped-comment analysis.

scope_mismatch_1404.root_cause: scope_mismatch is the highest-count gap type (1,404 instances). Source review found no actual ADL or using-namespace collisions. Pattern appears to be triggered by every qualified name (e.g., std::lock_guard, boost::asio::) that the scanner interprets as a potential scope conflict. Recommend removing this pattern from future scans or adding a whitelist for stdlib/boost qualifiers.
